narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 91.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong likelihood of failure led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3 pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. These rankings were far below the average of accepted students, who typically placed around the middle of their class. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, compared to an average of 3.23 among accepted applicants, and your LSAT score of 31 versus an average of 37.18, further reinforced this outlook, though they carried less weight than your class standing.

Your family's upper-middle income level also contributed to the prediction of failure, though to a smaller degree. While this bracket is common among accepted students, in your specific combination of factors it slightly increased the estimated risk.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Building a stronger record in law school coursework or gaining relevant experience could also help demonstrate your potential for success on the bar exam in a future application.
